en: God has struck it down!
These plane trees and willows standing here—
The people of Bukhara enjoyed their bounty.
‘This is Kanykei's Ken-Kolchuk,
Where the sovereign dwelt,’ they used to say.
Mother, the place where I played as a child,
Where your son came as a bridegroom
And took this poor soul as his wife.
Nine hundred piebald mares were slaughtered,
Nine khans and their peoples were invited,
And fame spread among the gathered people.
Wrestlers wrestled ninety days at my wedding feast;
This was the place where khans witnessed my feast.
Nine camel-loads of gold,
By Muslim custom,
The young wives gathered together
And divided as gifts to the bridal go-betweens.
Nine khans played the wedding ransom game,
In this place of ninety days' rejoicing.
Gold by the pood, precious gold—
This was where it was awarded as prizes.
The people gathered and acclaimed it;
This was where they came to me, the unfortunate one.
My father Temir Khan
Had the treasury opened.
Then, issuing orders to the people,
He scattered many gold coins.
Fat wethers were slaughtered.
Dervishes came to my wedding feast and ate their fill.
This was a place left as a memorial.
Parted from my abundance,
Fleeing to Bukhara,
I was the luckless woman!”
Then the bygone age, the departed days,
As I thought, came into my mind.
The fierce woman could not remain, sobbing.
From upon Taitoru,
Losing consciousness, with a thud,
Fierce Kanykei fell.
For the time it takes meat to cook,
She did not raise her head.
Speaking courage to her, giving her strength,
Chyiyrdy stood pleading:
“Do not weep, Kanykei,
Do not sob, my foal.
No craftsman makes what cannot break;
God creates no one who cannot die.
Sobbing will bring no remedy;
Manas cannot be found through howling.
Sobbing will bring no benefit.
Before this, Kanykei,
Many and varied peoples have passed away.
From this bottom-fallen false world,
Many kinds of lions have passed away;
Whole peoples have passed away.
Look, so many mighty ones have passed away.
Oh, Kanykei, raise your head.
Your lake's drying up
Means the death of your fierce wolf Manas.
Your poplars' withering
Means humiliation brought upon you,
And many swine dividing your livestock.
Oh, Kanykei, my foal,
Your plane trees' withering
Means your trotting like a hunting hound,
Bearing suffering, Kanykei,
And wandering here from Talas!
Your palace's collapse
Means your time of fortune has left you,
And your slaves slashed your breast open.
Turn to God, my child, raise your head.
Do you not see, Kanykei,
The falseness of this faithless world?
Semetey, left by the warrior—
Do not grieve, my foal.
Let us bind him to our waist as a keepsake.
Oh, Kanykei, my foal,
Do not torment yourself; raise your head.
Let us mark out and cast an omen.
For this child Semetey,
Whether his bond will be strong,
Let us cast an omen for our gift!
This lake of yours standing here,
Oh, Kanykei, my foal,
Is a place endowed with sanctity.
Do not be sad, Kanykei;
Your bloodthirsty Manas cannot be found.
Your lamenting is fitting.
Oh, Kanykei, my foal,
The saints gathered together
At this Ken-Kolchuk;
It was a place where they played.
The host of Baabedin and true Khyzyr,
Oh, Kanykei, my foal,
At this lake standing here—
It was where they performed ablutions.
In the middle of the lake,
At the place where the spring used to rise,
If I speak, my words to Allah are a lament.
Mounded like a wooden cauldron-case,
My precious Kanykei,
There is a patch of black turf.
Oh, my precious Kanykei,
Dip your hands into the water.
Beseeching the holy ones,
Perform the washing of your hands!
My precious foal,
Turn over the black turf.
Saying, ‘Leopard Manas, give me your aid,’
Overturn it toward the north!
If water wells abundantly from within,
It means God has granted us favor.
If there is no water within—
Oh, Kanykei, my foal,
It means God has struck us down!
For the only child, growing capable,
Kanykei, let us try casting an omen.
If your omen does not come true,
Following your lord Manas,
My child, let us both die together!”
Thus she spoke,
The elder woman, like a lord,
Now gave her words of divination.
Ah, the lord's wife Kanykei
Sprang up from her place.
Draping the gray belt firmly about her neck,
Her betrothed, Sultan Manas—
She beseeched his spirit.
“O God, set my affairs right!” she said.
Protect my orphan!” he said.
She dipped her hands into the water,
Performed the washing of her hands,
And dipped her feet into the water.
Your sister-in-law wept bitterly
And performed the washing of her feet.
The dark turf her mother Chyiyrdy had spoken of—
The poor slavewoman left by Manas,
Merciless terror in days gone by
She had indeed inflicted,
Your champion Manas Khan's polished spear,
Placed in her hands as a gift,
Kanykei, the suffering woman,
Had brought it with her.
One hand's breadth was ridged,
One hand's breadth was painted;
From meadowsweet and serviceberry
She had it turned with tireless labor.
Saying, ‘The middle will remain hollow,’
Kanykei, the formidable woman,
Had glue poured into it.
Thrust forth, it never drew back from an enemy;
Six thousand Chinese, countless governors,
With Khan Joloi laying siege,
When they closed in all around,
Struck, it never recoiled from iron;
Thrust in fury,
It split dark stone in two.
That skilled smith Bolokbai
Had fashioned the precious polished spear.
Your treasured sister-in-law, without stopping,
Gripped it with all her might.
Slanting it toward that turf,
Your sister-in-law, blessed by Khizyr, went forward.
Weeping in anguish, crying, ‘My lord!’
With a dull thud into its side,
Your poor sister-in-law Kanykei
Stood driving it in.
To the one Allah who commands all,
She offered her supplication.
The dark turf she had pierced—
She overturned that dark turf.
Your poor leopard sister-in-law
Turned it over toward the north.
When she turned it over, from that turf
A spring bubbled up with a gurgle.
To her leopard warrior Manas,
To his spirit she prayed;
Your dear sister-in-law Kanykei
Ran back, crying out.
It swelled and rippled into a pool;
The place she had marked filled up.
Its little lake was full now;
It had grown green again,
The plane tree's branches bending.
‘True divine power has granted this!’
The fierce woman cried out in joy.
The trees had all grown green;
When your poor sister-in-law looked,
A nightingale had perched atop them.
The nightingale sang and trilled;
Alas, its song was unbearable for a sorrowful soul.
The two ladies wept bitterly,
Unable to move a span from its roots.
Kanykei's Ken-Kolchuk
Had filled with water once again.
When the hapless woman was a girl,
The plane tree where she used to play
Was as it had been before.
The two ladies looked
At the plane tree standing there;
Their hearts brimmed like a lake.
Its leaves were like leather,
Its black worms the size of thumbs.
At the plane tree standing there,
Their poor little souls rejoiced.
At these things restored again,
Having witnessed such joy,
They prayed earnestly to God.
Then your wretched mother Chyiyrdy,
The saint protected by Shay,
The old woman who bore Manas,
Slung her belt around her neck
And wailed like a camel calf,
Pleading with Kanykei:
‘My dear Kanykei,
Surely God will ease our sorrow,
Surely Heaven will lift our grief.
Your hawk, your fortified city,
Will surely return to perch upon your hand.
Do not grieve, my foal;
Semetey, whom we look to for support,
Will surely become a leopard like his father!
The notched steel will be made whole;
Your spring flowing from the ridge,
Your dear child left by the champion,
Your tender gray-mottled falcon,
Your gray goshawk, your morning star.
The hardship and grief within us,
Let us blow them all away.
For this dear child left by the dead,
Let us pray to the one God.
Bring the provisions, my child;
Let us eat our fill as a thanksgiving offering.
To God, whose command is mighty,
My foal, let us offer a prayer!’
Dear, fierce Kanykei—
Kanykei then said:
‘My dear mother,
Before we reach Great Bukhara,
The vast Ak-Chii of broad Bukhara
For a good rider on a winged steed
Was a journey of six days.
There is no mountain the size of a knucklebone,
No hollow the size of a saddlecloth,
No furrow where a plow has passed,
No burrow dug by a marmot.
It looms in misty corners,
Its points dissolve in haze.
Ridge upon ridge lies ahead;
Land of terrible hardship lies ahead.
If a swan passes, its ears
Are burned in that land;
If a wild ass passes, its hooves
Are burned in that desert.
There is no grass to nibble,
No water for a single drop.
